claims.claim: No wealth tax is levied in Germany

sources.name: PwC: Germany, other taxes
sources.says: Last reviewed 30 June 2026. "At this point of time, no wealth taxes are levied in Germany." Inheritance and gift tax rates run from 7% to 50%, with tax-free amounts between EUR 20,000 and EUR 500,000 by relationship; tax applies when the testator, donor, heir or donee is a German tax resident, and otherwise only to German-situated assets.

claims.claim: Dividends, interest and capital gains pay a flat 25% plus the 5.5% solidarity surcharge (26.375%), plus church tax for members

sources.name: PwC: Germany, income determination
sources.says: Last reviewed 30 June 2026. Dividends, interest and capital gains from financial investments pay "a flat tax rate of 25% plus 5.5% solidarity surcharge (in total 26.375%, plus church tax if applicable)". The investor's allowance is "EUR 1,000 per taxpayer for the total of all financial investment income", "doubled in the case of married taxpayers filing jointly". Funds that retain profits "can trigger deemed income to be taxed at the investor level even if no actual distributions are made."

sources.name: PwC: Germany, taxes on personal income
sources.says: Last reviewed 30 June 2026. "All resident individuals are taxed on their worldwide income." A 5.5% solidarity surcharge applies in full to capital investment income; church tax is "either 8% or 9% of the income tax, depending on the federal state". The page describes no special regime for new residents, expatriates or retirees.

claims.note: Not in the profile and not added: Germany taxes fund investors each year on a deemed amount (Vorabpauschale) when a fund distributes little. A Dechert note of July 9, 2026 (https://www.dechert.com/knowledge/onpoint/2026/7/germany-s-advance-lump-sum-taxation--vorabpauschale---considerat.html, read 2026-11-15) gives 70% of the 3.20% base rate, 2.24% of opening value for 2026, capped at the year's actual gain, with 30% exempt for equity funds, and says it applies to foreign funds of contractual or corporate type; it does not address US-domiciled ETFs by name. A buy-and-hold ETF portfolio probably pays this each year, but no page read confirms it for US ETFs, so the fact was left alone. Worth a line in the profile if a later check settles it.

claims.modelMismatch: src/data/localTaxes.ts has no DE entry (its header lists Germany among countries with "no researched tax data"), so the simulation applies no German tax to Berlin. Checked facts for stage 8. No wealth tax (PwC, https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/germany/individual/other-taxes). Inheritance tax: the worldwide estate when the deceased or the heir is resident in Germany (ErbStG § 2, https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/erbstg_1974/__2.html); €400,000 allowance per child (§ 16); class I rates 7% to €75k, 11% to €300k, 15% to €600k, 19% to €6M, 23% to €13M, 27% to €26M, 30% above, each applied to the whole taxable amount, not marginally (§ 19, with step relief in (3)). claims.claim: Under the US–Germany estate and gift tax treaty (1998 protocol) a US citizen who is not German and has lived in Germany 10 years or less is treated as US-domiciled, so Germany generally taxes only German-sited assets left to US-resident heirs until then

sources.name: US Senate Executive Report 106-10: protocol amending the estate and gift tax convention with Germany
sources.says: November 3, 1999, on the protocol signed December 14, 1998. The protocol would "extend from five to ten years the period" of the citizenship exception: "a U.S. citizen who is domiciled in both the United States and Germany" under each country's law, and domiciled in Germany for not more than 10 years, "would be deemed to be domiciled only in the United States". The domicile country may tax worldwide and credits the other's tax on property there; the other country may tax certain situs assets such as real property and the business property of a permanent establishment.

sources.name: Taxes for Expats: Germany inheritance tax for US expats and heirs
sources.says: Last updated Oct 29, 2026. Children and stepchildren have a €400,000 allowance (ErbStG § 16, class I). The page does not describe the ten-year citizenship rule.

claims.note: Read in the Senate committee report rather than the treaty or the Treasury technical explanation the profile cites (a PDF). The report says "not more than 10 years", which matches "10 years or less". "German-sited assets" stands for the report's situs assets (real property, business property of a permanent establishment). A German-resident heir is taxed whatever the decedent's treaty domicile, which is why the profile says "US-resident heirs"; a German law firm's summary of a Federal Fiscal Court ruling to that effect appeared in a search result and was not read.
